title: The Wallet on the Bus
text:
On Tuesday evening I found a brown wallet under the seat on the number twelve bus.

My first thought was to [[ignore]] it. The bus was crowded, I was already late, and somebody else would surely pick it up. Then I thought about the face of the person who had lost it, and I could not [[accept]] that excuse.

I asked the driver what to do. He told me to [[report]] it at the station office, and he wanted me to [[describe]] exactly where the wallet had been.

The clerk at the office was patient. She asked me to [[complete]] a short form — where, when, and what the wallet looked like — and then to [[print]] my name clearly at the bottom.

Inside there were two bank cards, a student card and nine hundred dollars. The clerk did not [[blame]] me for opening it; she said anyone would have done the same.

"Most people just [[avoid]] this kind of trouble," she said. "It takes twenty minutes and you get nothing for it."

I told her I did not [[expect]] anything. I only wanted the owner to [[receive]] it back.

Three days later my phone rang. A university student had come to [[search]] for the wallet barely an hour after I handed it in. She wanted to [[offer]] me a reward, and I had to [[refuse]] three times before she finally believed me.

Then she said something I still [[remind]] myself of. She had almost stopped believing strangers, and one small thing had changed her mind for a whole year.

I did nothing clever that day. I did not [[solve]] a crime or save a life. I simply did not walk away.

title: Two Months Before the Science Fair
text:
Our group of four had two months to [[produce]] something for the science fair, and for three weeks we did almost nothing at all.

We could not agree on a topic. Wei wanted to [[invent]] a machine. Ting wanted to [[compare]] the water in four different rivers. We would [[argue]] about it for an hour after school and then go home.

Our teacher finally made us [[divide]] the work between us. "Stop trying to [[create]] one perfect idea," she said. "Choose the smaller one, and then [[improve]] it a little every week."

We chose the rivers. Every Saturday we went out to [[gather]] samples in small glass bottles, and Ting made me [[arrange]] them by date before we went home. Wei built a rough filter to [[detect]] the dirt we could not see with our eyes.

Slowly the project began to [[develop]] a shape of its own. The numbers from week one did not [[match]] the numbers from week four, and that difference turned into the whole story: the water below the factory got worse after every heavy rain.

On the evening before the fair our poster was still half empty. We stayed in the classroom until nine, and nobody had to [[suggest]] staying — we all simply did.

At the fair the judges asked us to [[discuss]] what had surprised us most. Wei answered first, and for once he did not talk too much.

We did not win. We came fourth. But all four of us agreed to [[continue]] the study next year, with better bottles and an earlier start.

title: The Night the Lights Went Out
text:
The radio began to [[broadcast]] the typhoon warning at six in the morning.

By eight the school had decided to [[cancel]] every class. My mother did not [[waste]] a single minute. She sent my brother out to [[lock]] the back gate and told me to [[shut]] every window on the second floor.

"Tape the glass," she said. "It will not stop a typhoon, but it may [[protect]] you from the pieces."

My father came home at ten with rice, eggs and a box of candles. Shops cannot [[provide]] anything once the wind really starts, he said, and we must not [[depend]] on the power staying on.

By midnight the wind had begun to [[shake]] the metal door at the back of the house. At two the lights went out.

My grandmother sat by the window and did not look worried at all. She told us how her village had to [[survive]] three days without any help in 1959, and how neighbours would [[support]] one another with whatever food was left.

Her voice did [[calm]] my little sister, who had been crying since the room went dark. My mother would [[insist]] that we eat properly even by candlelight, so we had rice and eggs at a table we could barely see.

By morning the wind had dropped. Branches, roof tiles and one entire bicycle lay across our street. Neighbours came out early to [[lift]] the heavy branches off the road, and nobody waited to be asked.

It took two more days for the water to [[return]] to the taps. I did not [[realize]] until then how much an ordinary quiet morning is worth.
